original: "I made it a fine hill with a fine view," I said, "and a great deal too much quiet to leave alone. I mean to build on it."
revised: "It is a perfectly fine hill with a fine view," I said, "and a great deal too much quiet to leave alone. I would build on it.”

snip: We walked the whole of it, that afternoon, the long slow way round, the way you walk a thing you mea
original: We walked the whole of it, that afternoon, the long slow way round, the way you walk a thing you mean to be answerable for. Cael went at the pace his knees allowed and I was glad of it, because it was the right pace for the ground, slow enough to see. He showed me the spring that came up cold and clear out of the hill's south face and had never once, in living memory or his grandmother's, gone dry; a thing worth more than the hill on top of it, he said, and he was right, and I would have cause to bless that spring a hundred times in the years after. He showed me the woodland strip, good mixed timber, oak and ash and a stand of larch a former owner had planted and not lived to cut. He showed me where the grade eased along the eastern slope into a shelf of deeper, greener grass, and I felt something about that shelf that I had not the knowledge yet to name and did not mention, and Cael did not mention it either, though I caught him watching me not mention it. And all the while the boy Soren went ahead of us and to the side, quiet as weather, stopping now and then to crouch over some particular patch of ground with the total absorption of a child at his real work, and once, near the crown, he stood for a long moment with his bare hand flat on a stone, and then took it off, and came on, and said nothing, and I thought nothing of it, which is a thing I would give a good deal to go back and un-think.

snip: And there is this, besides. Once in a great while, in some inn a long way from anywhere, I will hear
original: And there is this, besides. Once in a great while, in some inn a long way from anywhere, I will hear a story told that I half recognize, the way you might recognize your own coat on a stranger three sizes too large for it. There are not many of them. I am not, whatever you may have been led to expect, a man they sing about; I took a good deal of quiet care, over the years, that it should stay so. But a few tales got loose all the same, and time and retelling have warped them so far out of true that the man in them is half myth and half plain nonsense, and I would not know him to nod to in the road, and, if I am honest, do not much care for him. I hold the tellers no grudge; a good story is a kind of coin, and it is meant to be spent. It only seems a poor thing to leave nothing behind but those few, and so, if only so that the truth of it should exist somewhere, in one place, I mean to set down what actually happened. Or near enough. I will not pretend the years have warmed no words nor softened any faces; fondness does that, and I was fond of very nearly all of them, and they are gone now, every one of them, but me. Still, the shape of it is true, and the shape is the thing that matters.

original: I heard the story of myself again last night, told across a crowded taproom by a man who had no notion he was telling it to the one it belonged to, and I have been turning it over ever since, the way you turn a stone you picked up without meaning to and now cannot quite bring yourself to set down.

snip: I did not know him, the man in the story. That is the plain truth of it, and plain truth is very nea
original: I did not know him, the man in the story. That is the plain truth of it, and plain truth is very near all I have left that is worth the giving. They had made me into someone in those tales: a figure, a wonder, a man who walked through the whole of his life already knowing the shape of it. In the tale he came up the valley already meaning the tower, saw the whole of it standing behind his eyes on the first morning, and raised it in a season, and the hill made no argument. He was never once wrong about a footing, never sat a winter counting silver, never stood in the rain arguing with a wagon. The tellers are fond of such men. And the man they made is, if I may say so of my own story, no one I ever met. Sure of himself. Untouched by anything. Always the right word ready on his lips and never a wrong night lying behind him. I would not cross a room to shake his hand, and I have yet to hear the tale told in a way that made me wish I would.

snip: I had never meant to stay in it long, for that matter. Coming home to my father's house was to be a
original: I had never meant to stay in it long, for that matter. Coming home to my father's house was to be a stopgap, a place to keep myself and my boots while my own house went up across the river; and my own was to be a wonder, or a warning, depending on which of us you asked about it afterward: grander than anything my father would have put his name to, taller, flashier, altogether more foolish, the same clean lines he had given my mother swollen to twice the scale and three times the cost, a great bright thing built to stand as a gift and a grand gesture ahead of a wedding. I had drawn a good part of it myself, in the good years, when I still supposed I knew what I was building toward. There was no wedding, in the end, and so no need of the house. I never lived in it. For three years it had stood across the water full of a life that had not happened, costing me a small fortune a year in the bare keeping of a grand thing that nobody used, and I could no more sell it than cross its threshold. Penworth had spent the better part of that winter trying, with a delicacy that cost him something to keep up, to talk me round to letting it go, for the sake of my purse and, though he was too careful a man to say it, for the sake of the rest of me; and I had spent the winter not answering him.

snip: The first and easier part of it I had come by rail: three days out of Vethmark in a carriage that ra
original: The first and easier part of it I had come by rail: three days out of Vethmark in a carriage that rattled the teeth in a man's head and let the cold in at every seam. The railways were new then, and it showed. The engine that hauled us was a crude, soot-breathing thing, all iron and steam and appetite, and there was next to nothing of the arcane in it, which surprised the sort of people who supposed a wizard must approve of a train on principle. I did not, particularly. You may put a working into a machine, and I have put a good many into a good many; but a working has to be fed and tended and coaxed and renewed, and one big enough to shoulder a train up a grade would have eaten more in the keeping than the coal it saved. That is the arithmetic people get backwards about my trade. There is no shortage of magic in this world; there has never been a shortage of magic. What the world is short of is people who can work it. The talent is born, not made. The Conclave sharpens it where it appears, and it appears seldom, and more seldom than it once did. Coal the world has by the mountain, iron by the shire, stokers by the thousand for the hiring; of those born able to set a lasting working into iron it has a scattered handful, every one of them wanted in six places at once. Put the whole of that little company to nursing locomotives and you might keep one railway arcane, and nothing else in the world would ever be warded or mended or lit again. So no sane man spends a wizard where a stoker will serve, and the railways ran on fire and water and brute iron cleverness and almost no magic at all, and I spent a fair part of those three days watching the engine hiss and labor at the watering-stops and thinking, in the idle, itching way of a man who cannot let a made thing alone, how much smaller and quieter and cleverer the whole of it could have been built, if the world had only had the hands to spare for it. It did not. It never has. That is the first hard fact of my trade, and the trains were a great smoking monument to it: a mountain of crude iron doing loudly and dearly what a very little good artifice could have done well, had there only been enough good artifice to go around, which there was not, and is not, and I have stopped expecting there ever to be.

snip: The inn stood where the street widened toward the beck. It was a broad, comfortable-looking building
original: The inn stood where the street widened toward the beck. It was a broad, comfortable-looking building of three storeys, one of the few in Ardenmoor to stand so tall, with a painted sign gone too weathered to read and lamplight already spilling out of its windows into the blue evening. I have stopped at a great many inns and could write a dull and honest book on the subject. This one, before I had so much as got down off my horse, had the one quality that matters and cannot be built on purpose: it looked like somewhere a tired man might stop being tired for a while. I got down, and my legs told me at length exactly how far we had come. A boy came out of the inn-yard shadows to take Snow's head with the unhurried competence of a child who has been around horses since before he could walk.

original: Cael came in on the tail of the meal, the cold of the evening still on his shoulders and his grandson at his heel. original: There was no thread of fate in it, whatever a story would want. I did not come to Ardenmoor drawn by anything grander than an errand. I came because Penworth had an unerring eye and I had learned to trust it over my own; because it was spring, and I had spent the whole of the winter shut up in a quiet Vethmark townhouse with the spare rooms closed and sheeted, keeping well out of the way of the noise and the standing crowd of small obligations that a city presses on a man whether he asks for them or not, and had barely marked the season going by; and because there was nowhere else in the wide world I would rather have been, which in those days was less a boast than a fairly bleak measure of how small my life had got. *A hill of no agricultural worth and considerable quiet.* When I read that, it sounded like very nearly the only thing left that I wanted.

snip: Penworth was my man of affairs, and the running of my whole tangled life had been his for something
original: Penworth was my man of affairs, and the running of my whole tangled life had been his for something over a decade by then. He kept the letters, the monies, and the small steady mountain of paper any working life throws off whether a man attends to it or not. He was a spare, precise, exceedingly formal gentleman out of Vethmark, near enough my own age and a good deal tidier about the wearing of it, and he had a particular genius, earned across a long career spent in the disorder of other men's affairs, for finding me things before I knew I wanted them, and for quietly buying the ground under a thing while I was still making up my mind about the thing itself. His letter had reached me at the turn of the year, and I had carried it about ever since, folded twice and gone soft at the creases from a season in my coat. It was a small marvel of its kind: three close pages to tell me he had come across a piece of country he believed would suit me, *a hill of no agricultural worth and considerable quiet*; that he had taken the liberty of securing it provisionally, along with a good breadth of the workable land about it, the sort you could set to honest tenants and thereafter forget you owned; and that he would count it a personal kindness if I would go and look at what I had nearly purchased before he made me finish the purchasing.

original: The townhouse I had wintered in was my father's before it was mine, and my father had been an architect, which is to say a man who drew the houses that other men then lived their whole lives inside of. He had built up a small firm about the doing of it, a good and unglamorous one that outlived him and stands drawing houses yet, and I hold his share in it still, though I have not troubled it in years and it has had the grace not to trouble me. original: The house he kept for himself he had drawn years before, for my mother, early, when the firm was still more hope than trade and he built as much for the love of the thing as for the money in it. It was the finest small thing he ever set his hand to, and it stood in what had then been a quiet, unfashionable quarter of the city, the sort of street a young man of modest means could still afford a corner of. The quarter had not stayed unfashionable. The town had grown up around it in the years since, gone dear and grand, tall bright houses rising to either side until my father's modest little place sat among them like an honest word in an ornate sentence, worth many times over what it had cost him to raise and not a coin of that worth for anything he would have troubled to count. When the two of them were gone it came to me, and I had grown up in those rooms and been happy in them, in the years when the house smelled of drawing-ink and my mother's baking and the windows stood open on the garden half the year, and I came back to them, after everything, the way a man goes back to the one place that never once asked him to be anything more than he was.

original: The line gave out, as such lines do, exactly where the paying traffic did, at a raw and cheerful town called Wainford that lived to pour the country's grain and cattle into railway cars and held no higher opinion of itself.
